title: Astronomy and the Astrolabe
objective: After this level you can explain how Islamic scholars studied the sky with astrolabes.
summary: The Greek astrolabe reached the Islamic world by the 8th century, found prayer times and the qibla, and was refined (al-Zarqali). Many star names come from Arabic.

cards.headline: Aldebaran, Betelgeuse, Vega, Altair: the night sky speaks Arabic.
cards.body: Look up tonight and you’re reading names adopted from Arabic. Behind them is a brass instrument that helped find the direction of Mecca and the five daily prayer times.

cards.headline: A Greek star-taker
cards.body: The astrolabe’s name is Greek, roughly “star-taker”, and it probably began around the time of the astronomer Ptolemy, in the 2nd century CE. A star map called the rete turned over a plate made for one latitude, and a sighting rule measured a star’s height to find the time. The astrolabe reached the Islamic world by the 8th century. Borrowed, yes. Left alone, no.

cards.headline: Refined for prayer and for everywhere
cards.body: In the Islamic world, astrolabes found the qibla, the direction of Mecca, and the five daily prayer times. Astronomers kept refining the design. In Toledo, al-Zarqali (1029–1100) made a universal astrolabe that needed no separate plate for each latitude, and as the Saphea Arzachelis it was widely used in medieval Europe. One instrument for every city: that’s an upgrade.
cards.callout: Invented by Greeks, refined in the Islamic world

cards.headline: Names in the sky
cards.body: Arab astronomers also translated the star descriptions of Ptolemy’s Almagest, a Greek catalog from around 150 CE. In the 10th century the Persian astronomer al-Sufi updated it with his own catalog, later translated into European languages. That’s how Aldebaran got its name: “the follower”, because it follows the Pleiades across the sky. Stargazers everywhere are quietly speaking Arabic.

cards.headline: The astrolabe: understood
learned: The astrolabe was a Greek invention
It reached the Islamic world by the 8th century
It found prayer times and the qibla
Many star names come from Arabic

questions.prompt: In the Islamic world, which religious task did astrolabes help with?

options.label: Copying the Qur’an in the right order
Calling people to prayer from minarets
Finding the qibla and the daily prayer times

questions.explanation: Astrolabes found the qibla, the direction of Mecca, and the five daily prayer times.

questions.prompt: Why is it wrong to say the Islamic world invented the astrolabe?

options.label: It was a Greek instrument that Islamic astronomers refined
It was invented in China and traded west
It was first built in medieval Europe
options.rationale: Europe got it later, partly via Toledo.

options.label: It was invented in India with the numerals

questions.explanation: The astrolabe began in the Greek world around Ptolemy’s time; Islamic astronomers refined it, as al-Zarqali did.

questions.prompt: Level 57’s doctors built on Galen’s ancient medicine. Whose ancient star catalogue did Arab astronomers translate and al-Sufi update?

options.label: Galen’s
options.rationale: Galen was a medical authority, not an astronomer.

options.label: Euclid’s
options.rationale: Euclid was translated in Baghdad, but not as a star catalogue.

questions.explanation: Arab astronomers translated the star descriptions of Ptolemy’s Almagest, and al-Sufi updated it, much as medieval medicine built on Galen.
